title: Round Hill is suing Suno and Anthropic for up to $1B apiece. It isn’t looking to settle.

reading.body:
This incident centers on a failure at the data-ingestion stage of AI development. Suno admitted its model was trained on essentially all music files on the internet, and reporting based on a hack identified YouTube, Deezer, and Genius as specific scraping sources. The core failure is that copyrighted recordings were used as training material without the rights holders' permission, and the system then produced outputs close enough to identifiable original works that record labels could demonstrate the resemblance by submitting AI-generated tracks as court evidence.

The failure is one of deployment without licensing controls at the training stage, combined with insufficient output filtering at the generation stage. A system that can reproduce near-identical versions of well-known songs when prompted with descriptive genre and artist cues has not been constrained to prevent reproduction of protected expression. Catching this would have required either cleared training data, systematic output testing against known recordings before public release, or both.

What is not established: the lawsuits and class actions are allegations, the GEMA ruling is a court finding specific to that jurisdiction, the Warner settlement is a negotiated resolution rather than a liability verdict, and no court in the United States has issued a final judgment on the central copyright claims against Suno or Udio.

summary:
Major record labels including Universal Music Group, Sony Music, Warner Music, and others have filed separate lawsuits against Udio and Suno, two popular AI music generators. The labels accuse both companies of scraping thousands of copyrighted songs without permission to train their AI models and of directly reproducing sections of famous recordings. The lawsuits involve music from artists like The Beatles, Michael Jackson, Mariah Carey, and Bruce Springsteen. The record labels claim both companies have been deliberately secretive about their training data and refused to disclose which songs were used.

To support their case, the record labels demonstrated they could recreate famous songs by using specific prompts describing the original music's style, genre, and era. They provided examples showing how prompts like "1954 rock and roll billy haley comets" generated outputs mimicking original songs, and how requesting "Mariah Carey contemporary r&b holiday" produced near-identical versions of "All I Want for Christmas Is You." The record labels submitted a thumbdrive of these AI-generated songs as evidence. Udio was sued in New York while Suno was sued in Massachusetts, setting up major legal battles over how generative AI services handle copyrighted material.
